characters: Kwame: a Ghanaian boy introduced at age fourteen in a JHS coding club in Accra (wearing a navy polo shirt) and later shown as a young software developer in his twenties.
Adwoa: Kwame’s classmate and co-founder, a sharp problem-solver with natural puffs and a cyan blouse, who leads operations, user research and technician training.
Master Ibrahim: a skilled vocational-school electrical and plumbing instructor in his forties, wearing a neat grey work jacket and carrying a multimeter.
Madam Akua: a busy bakery owner in Accra in her thirties, wearing a white apron over a colourful wax-print dress.

narrationPlan.voice: Engaging, contemporary Ghanaian narrator (en-GH); energetic for Kwame, thoughtful and clear for Adwoa and Master Ibrahim.
notes: Pronounce Kwame ("KWAH-meh"), Adwoa ("ah-JOH-ah"), Akua ("ah-KOO-ah") and Esi ("EH-see") clearly.

music: Optional subtle marimba and modern lo-fi synth pulse; off by default.
culturalNotes: Highlights the partnership between digital software entrepreneurship and Ghana’s vital Technical and Vocational Education and Training (TVET) artisans.
reviewQuestions: Does the story realistically portray the multi-year effort required to build a trusted tech-enabled business and create 100 jobs?

pages.brief: Split street view in Accra: on one side Madam Akua (white apron over wax-print dress) looking worried outside her bakery; on the other side young vocational graduates sitting with neat toolboxes beside Master Ibrahim (grey work jacket); Kwame (14, navy polo) and Adwoa (14, natural puffs, cyan blouse) observing both.
pages.narration: Set up the two-sided marketplace problem clearly: households/shops needing trusted repairs, and trained youth needing steady work.

pages.brief: School computer lab: Kwame and Adwoa typing eagerly at a laptop whose screen shows a complex, crowded layout of icons and video boxes (no readable text).
pages.narration: Show the classic beginner mistake: rushing to write code without customer discovery.

pages.brief: Outdoors by a workshop: a young technician holding a basic smartphone with a spinning loading wheel icon while Kwame and Adwoa look deflated beside their laptop.
pages.narration: Honest, relatable setback: why technology fails when it ignores real user constraints.

pages.brief: Inside Master Ibrahim’s vocational workshop: Adwoa and Kwame taking notes in paper notebooks as Master Ibrahim and Madam Akua point to a simple checklist and a multimeter.
pages.narration: Turning point: humility, listening and structured customer discovery.

pages.brief: University innovation hub: Kwame and Adwoa (now in their early twenties) testing a clean, minimal interface on a budget smartphone alongside a basic keypad phone (no readable text).
pages.narration: Show realistic multi-year skill growth and smart low-bandwidth engineering.

pages.brief: Clean office desk: Kwame working on a computer displaying a glowing padlock and shield icon over database blocks (no text), while Adwoa reviews a compliance binder.
pages.narration: Emphasise responsible software engineering and compliance with Ghana’s Data Protection Act (Act 843).

pages.brief: Bright technical training workshop: Master Ibrahim and Adwoa watching a young female electrician and a young male plumber complete a neat wiring and pipe test bench, wearing smart cyan-and-navy technician shirts.
pages.narration: Show that real tech businesses combine software with offline quality, training and safety.

pages.brief: Madam Akua smiling as she pays via mobile phone after her bakery mixer is fixed by a young female technician; a clean visual inset shows nine gold coins going to the technician and one coin going to the platform hub (no text).
pages.narration: Walk through the unit economics clearly: 100-cedi job = 90 cedis (90%) to the technician + 10 cedis (10%) platform fee.

pages.brief: Bustling operations room: Kwame monitoring green server health lights while Adwoa and customer-support staff in headsets assist technicians and customers on a map of southern and middle Ghana.
pages.narration: Realistic multi-year operational grit: backups, receipts, guarantees and gradual trust.

pages.brief: Wide celebratory courtyard photo in Accra: Kwame, Adwoa and Master Ibrahim surrounded by a joyful group of office staff (with laptops and headsets) and uniformed male and female technicians holding their toolkits.
pages.narration: Clear, celebratory arithmetic: 25 full-time staff + 75 certified technicians = 100 decent jobs created over 5 years.

pages.brief: Bright neighbourhood electrical workshop: Esi (22, cyan-and-navy technician shirt, safety glasses) showing two eager teenage apprentices how to test a solar inverter with a multimeter.
pages.narration: Show the multiplier effect of decent job creation and link back to Tier 3 pension habits.

pages.brief: Back in the JHS computer room: Kwame and Adwoa smiling warmly as JHS students work in pairs with both laptops and paper interview notebooks open on their desks.
pages.narration: Inspiring closing message grounding technology in human empathy, ethics and job creation.

teacherGuide.overview: A realistic JHS technology and entrepreneurship story showing how a software platform creates real economic value only when combined with customer discovery, inclusive low-bandwidth design (including USSD), data privacy under Ghana’s Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843), vocational skills verification, fair commission splits (90/10), and multi-year operational persistence.
learningGoals: Explain why customer discovery (interviewing users before coding) prevents wasted effort and failed products.
Describe how low-bandwidth design and USSD make digital services accessible across Ghana.
Explain why software builders must protect personal data under Ghana’s Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843).
Calculate marketplace revenue splits (90 cedis technician earnings + 10 cedis platform fee = 100 cedis) and total job creation (25 staff + 75 technicians = 100 jobs).

whatWeKnow: In software engineering, user-centred design and early customer discovery significantly reduce product failure rates.

In Ghana, the Data Protection Act, 2012 (Act 843) and the Data Protection Commission require organisations that process personal data to safeguard privacy, collect only necessary data, and keep records secure.
whatWeAreStillDiscovering: Computer scientists in West Africa are developing offline-first mobile architectures and voice-assisted interfaces in local languages so artisans and customers can transact reliably regardless of network quality.

investigation.title: Paper-Prototype Usability Test
materials: Two sheets of paper, a pencil, and a classmate who has not seen your drawing.
steps: On Sheet A, draw a cluttered "Version 1" phone screen with 12 tiny buttons and long paragraphs. On Sheet B, draw a clean "Version 2" screen with 3 clear choices.
Show Sheet A to your partner for 5 seconds and ask them how they would book an electrician. Time how long it takes them to find the right button.
Repeat with Sheet B and compare which design was faster, clearer, and needed less explanation.

pronunciation.guidance: Ghanaians often say "uh-KRAH" (stress on the second syllable).
"KWAH-meh". English speakers often say "KWAH-mee"; confirm the final vowel.
reviewerNotes: Confirm final vowel (meh vs mee) and the "kw" onset.

pronunciation.guidance: "ah-JWAH". The "dw" is the hard part for English engines and is probably not a plain "d" + "w".
reviewerNotes: HIGH RISK: the "dw" cluster. Native speaker to demonstrate and approve a rendering.
